market-structure.audience: Anyone who can open a chart and wants a vocabulary for what is on it. No prior technical analysis is assumed — Market Structure Lab starts from a bare candlestick chart — and no platform, account, or subscription is needed. The lessons stay useful if you already trade and want a stricter definition of invalidation.
market-structure.usage: Entries are placed on pullbacks defined by market structure, ranges, breakouts, liquidity sweeps, and multi-timeframe context. Stops are placed at the structural levels those concepts name, and options contract selection prices the plan built from invalidation, stops and reward-to-risk. Each lesson ends with a way to test yourself.

trade-setup-execution.audience: Anyone who can already read a chart and now wants a repeatable procedure for acting on one. Market Structure is the assumed background: this course places stops at structural levels and enters on pullbacks without stopping to define either. It also suits someone who trades already and cannot say, from records rather than memory, which of their setups actually pays.
trade-setup-execution.usage: Entry confirmation requires a named setup: breakout, pullback or reversal. Position sizing needs the stop distance established by stop-loss placement, and performance review needs records from the trading journal. Recording decisions and reviewing their outcomes makes the setup and execution work usable beyond an individual trade.

options-trading.audience: Anyone who can read a chart and now wants to understand the instrument that trades on top of it — including the reader who has bought a call, watched the stock go the right way, and still lost money. It starts from contract terms, so no prior options knowledge is assumed. It also suits someone who already trades options and cannot say, without guessing, which part of a premium is intrinsic and which part is the clock.
options-trading.usage: Delta, gamma, theta and vega only mean something once option premium has been split into intrinsic and extrinsic value. Options strategies assume you can price the legs. Options Trade Planning asks for a spread cost, a risk budget and an exit rule, using the calculations explained in these lessons. Planning connects knowledge of contracts and strategies to decisions about risk.

technical-indicators.audience: Anyone who has an indicator on their chart and could not, right now, write down its formula or say what makes it lag. It assumes you can read a chart and starts from the calculation, so no prior indicator knowledge is needed. It also suits the reader who has six indicators open and suspects — correctly — that four of them are showing the same thing twice.
technical-indicators.usage: Moving-average smoothing is the basis of the envelopes that use it. Indicator divergence needs the RSI, stochastic and MACD oscillators. Indicator-Based Trading Rules asks for trend, strength and volatility filters: moving-average trend filters, directional movement, ATR and the Bollinger, Keltner and Donchian channels. Reading, combining and selecting indicators connects their formulas to context.

volume-and-order-flow.audience: Anyone who has said "that breakout had volume" without being able to say volume relative to what. It assumes you can read a chart and know what a moving average does; it assumes nothing about order books, tape reading or delta. It also suits the reader who has a footprint chart open and is quietly unsure whether the green number means buyers were stronger — the course is explicit that every trade has both a buyer and a seller, and that aggressor classification describes which side crossed the spread, not an unequal number of participants.
volume-and-order-flow.usage: The relative-volume baseline comparison makes the volume-confirmation test meaningful. Session VWAP is the reference that anchored VWAP moves, and volume profile is what the value area is drawn on. Volume and Order Flow Trading Rules asks for market context, participation, location, aggressive flow and price confirmation. The tape and the book answer different questions: executed transactions and displayed intent.

trading-risk-management.audience: Anyone who can find a setup and cannot say what it is allowed to cost. It assumes you can read a chart, place a stop and tell a call from a put; it assumes nothing about expectancy, drawdown mathematics, margin mechanics or correlation. It also suits the reader who has been sizing positions by round numbers of shares and has quietly noticed that a wide stop and a narrow stop then risk wildly different amounts — the course is explicit that size is an output, computed from the risk you allowed and the distance to invalidation, and never an input you pick first.
trading-risk-management.usage: Account Risk and Risk Budget defines the budget that Risk Per Trade spends. Stop-Loss and Structural Invalidation defines the distance that Position Sizing divides by. R-multiples are the units of expectancy. Losing Streaks and Drawdown provides the drawdown context that makes Risk of Ruin a number rather than a worry. Execution risk distinguishes the loss planned from the loss actually taken. Trading Risk Plan asks for account limits, sizing, execution constraints, portfolio exposure, options rules and review triggers; those dependencies explain the concepts it draws on.

backtesting-and-trading-systems.audience: Anyone who has produced a beautiful equity curve and cannot say why it should be believed. It assumes you can read a chart, and that risk per trade, R-multiples, expectancy and drawdown already mean something to you — Trading Risk Management defines them. It assumes nothing about walk-forward analysis, Monte Carlo resampling or point-in-time data. It also suits the reader who has never written a backtest and wants to know what the result of one is worth: the honest answer is that a simulation is evidence about a past sequence, that costs and timing decide most of it, and that a curve fitted to the data it was chosen on is not evidence at all.
backtesting-and-trading-systems.usage: Testable trading rules are what historical data, point-in-time universes, bar construction and signal timing feed. Simulated fills and transaction costs produce the equity curve. Performance metrics require the sample size those metrics describe. The split between in-sample, validation and out-of-sample data makes walk-forward analysis and stress tests more than another look at the same fitted result. Validation distinguishes a search from a test.

algorithmic-and-automated-trading.audience: Anyone who has a rule set they trust and no idea what it takes to let it run unattended. It assumes you can read a chart, and that risk per trade, position sizing, expectancy and out-of-sample validation already mean something to you — Trading Risk Management and Backtesting and Trading Systems define them. It assumes nothing about distributed systems: idempotency, reconciliation, traces, secret rotation and rollback are introduced here, from the trading problem they solve rather than from the general engineering literature. It also suits the reader who has decided NOT to automate, and wants to know what they would be signing up for: most of this course is about failure — a timeout with unknown state, a duplicate order, a stale price, a credential with more permission than it needs — and none of that goes away because the strategy is good.
algorithmic-and-automated-trading.usage: Architecture defines the boundaries across which market data and clock events travel. Strategy state and risk limits constrain what broker calls and order management may do. Reliability, observability and security work must account for order status arriving out of order. A missing response creates an uncertain state that the system must reconcile; a good strategy alone does not resolve it.
